Abstract
Dietary choices significantly impact both human health and the environ-
ment, with food-related greenhouse gas emissions (GHGE) constituting
a major contributor to climate change. While broad dietary guidelines
advocate for reducing animal-based food consumption, these recom-
mendations often lack the specific and actionable direction to motivate
behaviour change. This study examines the effectiveness of specific and
actionable product swap recommendations - proposing plant-based alter-
natives in place of animal-based products - within an experimental
1

2
online supermarket setting. We further assess whether (1) a recom-
mendation targeting the most effective GHGE-reducing swap and (2)
proving GHGE reduction information alongside these recommendations
enhances their impact. Participants were overall receptive to receiv-
ing product swap recommendations. Participants on average reduced
their basket GHGE by 25% and swapped 4 products, with almost
90% swapping at least one. The targeted recommendation increased
the uptake of the most effective swap, but neither targeted recommen-
dations nor GHGE reduction translated into significantly lower basket
GHGE for the majority of participants. Exploratory analyses suggest
that GHGE reduction information has a notably positive impact on
daily meat consumers, resulting in lower basket GHGE, more prod-
ucts swapped, an increased willingness-to-swap meat products and in
increase in their self-efficacy to reduce animal-product consumption.
These findings suggest that offering consumers the option to swap prod-
ucts—without the need for targeted recommendations or GHGE informa-
tion—may already be sufficient to encourage more sustainable purchasing
behaviours for many. However, to influence high-impact consumers,
particularly those with frequent meat consumption, providing GHGE
reduction information may be necessary to facilitate behaviour change.
1 Introduction
Food choices have both near and far reaching effects on human health and the
environment. Near to the individual, poor dietary choices are a leading cause
of morbidity and mortality [1, 2] and are a major contributor to a household’s
environmental impact, with approximately 20-30% of a household’s overall
environmental impact stemming from food consumption [3] in the European
union. Further from the individual, food choices exert significant pressure on
global healthcare systems, ecosystems, and agriculture [4–7], and contribute
substantially to greenhouse gas emissions (GHGE) [2, 8, 9], water pollution,
and more environmental impacts. Current consumption trends, particularly
high intake of animal-based foods [10], jeopardize the attainment of the 1.5°C
and 2°C climate targets established by the Paris Agreement [11].
Shifting from diets rich in animal-based products to those incorporating
more plant-based foods is a key strategy for reducing dietary carbon footprints
[8] while simultaneously lowering the risk of diet-related diseases [2, 7, 8, 12–
14]. However, dietary change remains challenging [15, 16], as food choices are
deeply rooted in taste preferences, traditions [16, 17], lifestyles [15, 18, 19],
and sociocultural contexts [15, 20–22].
Dietary guidance to reduce environmental impacts generally advocates for
animal-based food consumption and increasing plant-based food intake. How-
ever, general diet-level recommendations can be challenging to translate into
specific food choices [23, 24] due to limitations in nutrition literacy [25], a lack

3
of specific and actionable direction to trigger behaviour change [26, 27] and
often demand drastic and unrealistic dietary changes [24].
An alternative approach is promoting small, targeted dietary changes. Such
modifications are often more feasible for consumers, cater to a broader audi-
ence, and enhance self-efficacy compared to more extreme dietary shifts, such
as adopting vegetarian or vegan diets [2]. Simulation-based studies suggest
that even minor dietary adjustments, such as replacing 10% of beef-derived
caloric intake with select plant-based foods [24] or substituting high-carbon
with lower-carbon meats (e.g., chicken instead of beef) [2], can achieve substan-
tial reductions in dietary carbon footprints (33–35%) while yielding meaningful
health co-benefits.
Consumers prefer dietary guidance that is specific, actionable, and relevant
to their daily lives [26, 27]. Research on the Dietary Guidelines for Ameri-
cans, for instance, found that abstract recommendations — such as limiting
fat intake to 30% of total calories — are perceived as impractical, as consumers
do not want to perform complex calculations when making food choices [26].
In this regard, small targeted changes need to be translatable into meaning-
ful specific and actionable guidance. For instance, while consumers can benefit
both environmentally and nutritionally by “substituting 10% of caloric intake
from beef and processed meat for fruits, vegetables, nuts, legumes and selected
seafood” [24], working in caloric percentages is impractical and not a guideline
that consumers could easily follow [26]. Consumers favour clear specific direc-
tions that are meaningful to their lives that do not require calculations [26],
such as product swap recommendations [2, 27].
Simulation-based studies suggest that targeted product swap recommen-
dations hold significant potential for reducing dietary GHGE [2, 28]. A study
simulating product swaps using Swiss household grocery purchase data found
that swapping just one targeted animal-based product per shopping trip could
reduce basket GHGE by nearly 30% on average (for baskets containing animal-
based products) and lower overall household GHGE from food purchases by
26% [28]. The targeted product swap recommendation is derived from the final
contents of a shopping basket and targets the product that, when swapped,
would result in the greatest GHGE reduction. Comparatively, the second and
third most effective swaps only reduced household GHGE by 7% and 3%,
respectively [28].
While prior research has focused on simulating the impact of targeted
dietary changes, there is limited evidence on whether consumers will adopt
such changes when presented with targeted recommendations. Field evidence
from the energy sector suggests that targeted, high-impact interventions —
such as strategies focused on water heating and air-conditioning — result
in greater reductions in energy consumption than interventions addressing a
broad set of activities, such as reducing total household electricity use [29, 30].
However, dietary behaviour presents unique challenges, and it remains unclear
whether targeted dietary recommendations will be more effective in driving
behaviour change compared to offering a broader set of substitution options.

4
If a targeted recommendation conflicts with an individual’s taste preferences
or budget constraints, it may be disregarded. Conversely, providing multiple
options allows individuals to select those that best align with their preferences,
even if they are not the most effective in reducing GHGE. Ultimately, sub-
optimal but accepted changes would yield greater benefits than optimal but
unadopted recommendations.
Providing consumers with information about the environmental impact
of their food choices is a key intervention for promoting climate-friendly
behaviour. While nutrition fact labels are already established, sustainabil-
ity labels have also been shown to support more environmentally conscious
food choices [31–33]. However, research has yet to explore whether present-
ing GHGE reduction information alongside specific, actionable product swap
recommendations enhances their effectiveness.
Providing information on the environmental impact of different choices
could empower consumers by clarifying the magnitude of potential reductions
(e.g., “This swap reduces your GHGE by X%”). At the same time, product
swap recommendations may be more persuasive when paired with data quan-
tifying their effectiveness, as consumers often struggle to gauge which changes
make a meaningful impact [34]. While individuals may not always adopt the
most optimal strategy for reducing GHGE, information gives empowers them
to make informed trade-offs between personal preferences and environmental
outcomes.
This study investigates how specific and actionable product swap recom-
mendations, derived from the final contents of consumers’ shopping baskets
and presented before checkout, influence climate-friendly food choices. Addi-
tionally, it examines whether the combination of targeted product swap
recommendations and GHGE reduction information enhances the effectiveness
of these product swap recommendations.
In an online supermarket experiment environment, 1059 participants were
presented with a basket of products typical of the German consumer and
instructed to navigate through the supermarket to checkout. Prior to checkout,
participants were exposed to the product swap recommendations intervention.
The intervention consisted of product swap recommendations page with (1)
text explaining how swapping animal-based products for plant-based products
can meaningfully reduce the environmental impact of their food choices (Fig.
1(a)) and (2) a list of product swap recommendations from the animal-based
products in their basket to the closest matching second-generation plant-
based analogue equivalents (e.g. swap beef burger for plant-based burger).
Plant-based analogues were chosen for the swap recommendations due to their
inherent similarities to their animal-based counterparts. These products are
packaged, sold, prepared, and consumed in comparable ways, making them a
straightforward option for product swap recommendations and without neces-
sitating knowledge of new recipes or cooking methods. Additionally, there
is growing consumer acceptance of and demand for plant-based alternatives
[2, 35–37].

5
To examine the impact of targeted product swap recommendations and
GHGE reduction information in conjunction with specific and actionable prod-
uct swap recommendations, the participants were randomised to one of four
experimental conditions of a 2 x 2 experimental design. The two independent
factors were Targeted (Yes vs. No) and Information (Yes vs. No), shown in Fig.
1(b). The Targeted factor determines whether participants see the a targeted
product swap recommendation (i.e. the most effective GHGE-reducing product
swap) prominently highlighted as being the most effective. The Information
factor determines whether participants see alongside each swap recommenda-
tion the percentage reduction in their basket’s GHGE that would result from
swapping that product.
Participants could select as many of the available product swaps as they
desired. We evaluate the efficacy of the product swap recommendations as the
differences between the experimental conditions on shopping task outcomes,
such as final basket GHGE and swap recommendations selected. Addition-
ally, we analyse the recommendations effect on outcome variables collected
in the post-task survey, including participants’ receptivity to receiving prod-
uct swap recommendations, willingness-to-swap products, and self-efficacy and
response-efficacy regarding making dietary changes. Demographic and dietary
data were additionally collected to identify and explore differences among
subgroups. The study was preregistered and incentive compatible.

2 Methods
2.1 Design and procedure
To investigate the role the pre-checkout product swap recommendations to
reduce consumer food GHGE, and in particular, the role of offering targeted
swap recommendations and the role of providing GHGE reduction informa-
tion, we conducted a 2 x 2, between-subject, randomised controlled trial in
a simulated online supermarket environment. The study was pregistered and
incentive compatible. The study was ran over a period of 11 weeks. The study
and four experimental conditions were designed to investigate the following
hypotheses:
H1 Participants shop more climate-friendly after receiving product swap
recommendations from animal-based products to plant-based products.
H2 Participants shop more climate-friendly when the most effective GHGE
reducing product swap is highlighted compared to just offering product swap
recommendations from animal-based products to plant-based products.
H3 Participants shop more climate-friendly when the GHGE reduction
information of each product swap is displayed compared to just offering
product swap recommendations from animal-based products to plant-based
products.
H4 Participants shop more climate-friendly when the most effective GHGE
reducing product swap is highlighted, and this effect is stronger when the
GHGE reduction information of each product swap is displayed.
An initial survey was used to determine eligibility for the study and to
gather demographic, dietary and grocery purchasing data, and to randomise
participants to one of the four experimental conditions. At the end of the ini-
tial survey, eligible participants were informed about the shopping task and the
online supermarket. For incentive compatibility, participants were informed
that 10 participants would be randomly selected to receive the products they
purchased in the online supermarket, and as such, should choose their prod-
ucts carefully. The initial survey finished with an attention check to ensure
that participants understood there was a chance that they could receive the
products they chose. Upon passing the attention check, participants were redi-
rected to the online shopping platform for the shopping task.
The shopping task consisted of participants being presented a pre-selected
basket of 21 products representing the average German basket of a 2-person
household over a one-week period [38], covering cereals, meat, fish, dairy, eggs,
fruit, and vegetables. All products and product data, such as price, were taken
directly from a major German brick-and-mortar retailer that also has an online
supermarket. The look and feel of the online supermarket was also modelled on
the same retailers. Participants were instructed to proceed through the online
supermarket to checkout, as if they were doing their weekly grocery shopping.
Prior to checkout, participants landed on the intervention page where there was
an explanation on how swapping animal-based products for plant-based prod-
ucts can meaningfully reduce the environmental impact of their food choices,

8
and in addition, participants were then presented with a list of recommended
swaps from the 11 animal-based products in their basket to plant-based alter-
native products according to their prescribed experimental condition (outlined
below). Participants could select as many of the available product swaps as
they desired.
After the swaps recommendations intervention, participants were brought
to a final checkout page where their final basket was presented and completed
the shopping. Upon completion, participants were automatically redirected
to a post-task survey which was used to collect information on the par-
ticipants’ shopping experience, environmental concerns, willingness-to-swap
(WTS) products, familiarity with the swap recommendation products, rea-
sons why they did and did not swap products, as well as self-efficacy and
response-efficacy concerning reducing animal-product consumption. Partici-
pants received 3 GBP as compensation for a median study duration time of
approximately 12 minutes.
Greenhouse gas emissions data for products were adapted from [28], where
they were estimated using a bottom-up life cycle assessment (LCA) that inte-
grated data from product-specific sources and life cycle inventory databases.
The impact assessment for GHG emissions was derived from the Global Warm-
ing Potential (GWP) 100a [4], which takes into account all GHG emissions
that contribute to climate change, and for a time horizon of 100 years, each
greenhouse gas (carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide) is compared with the
climate impact of carbon dioxide and expressed in carbon dioxide equivalents.
A detailed description of the LCA methodology can be found in [28].

The study was approved by the University of Zurich Ethics Commis-
sion. The preregistration and the data of this study are publicly available
on the Open Science Framework project page (DOI: https://osf.io/nb4vt/
?view only=2d5ab97ba2ba4673843818f452098b3b). The study was conducted
online between July 28th and October 15th, 2023.
2.2 Participants
A sample of German-speaking participants was recruited via online panels
managed by Prolific. Preregistered exclusion criteria included (i) a minimum
age of 16 years, (ii) identify with a diet that restrict the consumption of animal
products (i.e. vegan or vegetarian), (iii) an answer of “never” for items con-
cerning their consumption frequency of dairy products and meat products, (iv)

9
failed attention checks, and (v) did not complete the pre-task survey, shopping
task, or post-task survey. Additionally, after data collection, we excluded non-
binary participants (N = 12) due to their low representation in the sample,
which prevented reliable statistical estimation.
The required sample size was calculated with a power of 0.8 and α of 0.05
to detect a small effect size (f2 = 0.02) with 3 predictors. This gives a total
sample size of 863 participants. To account for dropouts and missing data, we
increased the sample size to 1200 participants. Of these 1200 participants, 2 did
not complete the initial survey and 96 were excluded due to not meeting the
inclusion criteria. 1059 of these eligible participants completed the shopping
task and all of these participants completed the post-task survey. Table 4 shows
the demographic characteristics of the sample.
2.3 Intervention and experimental conditions
Participants were randomly exposed to one of four experimental conditions
of a 2 x 2 experimental design on the product swap recommendation page:
Targeted(Yes vs No) and Information(Yes vs. No), shown in Figure 1. In our
preregistration, we referred to the Targeted treatment as “Generic” vs. “Tar-
geted” and the Information treatment as “Without Information” vs. “With
Information”. In this manuscript, we use the new terminology “Targeted (No
vs. Yes)” and “Information (No vs. Yes)” for clarity and to better reflect the
nature of the interventions and their implementation in the statistical models.
The underlying conditions and experimental design remain unchanged.
Participants in all experimental conditions were exposed to the swap rec-
ommendation intervention that (1) explained how swapping animal-based
products for plant-based products can meaningfully reduce the environmental
impact of their food choices, and (2) presented a list of recommended swaps
from the 11 animal-based products in their basket to plant-based alterna-
tive products. The Targeted(Yes vs. No) treatments differed in that the most
effective GHGE reducing product swap (i.e., the targeted swap) was explic-
itly highlighted as being the most effective at reducing basket GHGE in the
Targeted(Yes) treatment. The Information(Yes vs. No) treatments differed in
that the percentage GHGE reduction that would occur from the swap was
displayed alongside each swap in the Information(Yes) treatment. The swap
recommendations were from the original animal-based product to it’s closest
second generation plant-based analogue. For example, plant-based sausages
were the recommended swap from pork-based sausages, and soy-based yoghurt
was the recommended swap from milk-based yoghurt. The recommended swap
products were chosen to be as close as possible in terms of product weight to
the original product in the basket (e.g. 500g of milk-based yoghurt could be
swapped for 500g of soy-based sausages). Where this was not possible, multi-
ple packages of the recommended swap product were recommended to match
the weight of the original product in the basket (e.g. a 350g package of chicken
could be swapped for two 180g packages of plant-based chicken).

2.4 Measures
The primary dependent variable was basket GHGE reduction following the
product swap recommendations intervention. This was calculated by determin-
ing the difference in GHGE of the initial basket (i.e. before the product swap
recommendations page intervention) and the final basket (i.e. after product
swap recommendations page intervention). The secondary dependent variables
were a binary variable for whether participants chose the targeted product
swap recommendation (i.e. the product recommendation that is highlighted in
Targeted treatment) and reported self-efficacy and response-efficacy regarding
reducing their animal product consumption. The items on perceived self-
efficacy and response-efficacy items were adapted from [39] and participants
were asked to indicate the level of agreement on a 7 point Likert scale from 1
(“totally disagree”) to 7 (“totally agree”). Item text are provided in the tables
reporting the results in the Appendix (Table 8 and Table 10).
Other preregistered exploratory variables included: receptivity to receiving
recommendations for alternative products with a lower their carbon footprint
when shopping (1 = “not at all” to 7 = “completely”); how well the supermar-
ket informed participants about which food in your shopping basket can reduce
their carbon footprint the most or the least (1 = “informed very poorly” to 7 =
“informed very well”); how well the supermarket informed participants about
the percentage reduction in carbon footprint that could achieved through each
product swap recommendation (1 = “informed very poorly” to 7 = “informed
very well”); percentage of their meat consumption they would be would be
willing to swap for plant-based alternatives (slider scale from 0 to 100); per-
centage of their dairy consumption they would be would be willing to swap
for plant-based alternatives (slider scale from 0 to 100).
In addition to the preregistered exploratory variables, we also report the
number of products that participants swapped and the number of participants
that swapped at least one product.
2.5 Statistical analysis
2.5.1 Preregistered analyses
To test Hypotheses 1–4, we conducted regression analyses. For the primary
analysis, we employed multiple linear regression, with percentage reduction in
GHGE as the dependent variable and the treatments Targeted (Yes = 1, No
= 0) and Information (Yes = 1, No = 0) as independent variables.
For the secondary analysis examining whether participants selected the
targeted swap recommendation, we used a logistic regression model, where the
dependent variable was a binary indicator of swap selection (Yes = 1, No =
0), and the same treatment variables were included as predictors.
Additionally, for the secondary analysis on self-efficacy and response-
efficacy, we conducted multiple linear regression models, using participant
ratings on these measures as dependent variables and the treatment conditions
as independent variables.

11
For our analyses, a p-value of less than .05 will indicate a significant
effect of the independent variables on our dependent variable. According
to our preregistration, we also examined the influence of covariates: diet
habits, gender, age and income. In the adjusted models including these covari-
ables, we included variables Daily Meat Consumer (Yes = 1, No = 0),
Daily Dairy Consumer (Yes = 1, No = 0), Gender (Male=1, Female=0),
Age (Years), Income (Euros). All models and code are publicly available
on the Open Science Framework project page (DOI: https://osf.io/nb4vt/
?view only=2d5ab97ba2ba4673843818f452098b3b).
2.5.2 Exploratory analyses
In addition to the preregistered analyses, we conducted post hoc exploratory
analyses to assess the effects of the Targeted and Information treatments
amongst participants who consume meat daily. This subgroup is of particular
interest, as they represent consumers with some of the highest dietary carbon
emissions.
Given the exploratory nature of these analyses, results should be inter-
preted with caution, and future studies should confirm these findings in
preregistered designs. To ensure robustness, we report only results where treat-
ment effects on daily meat consumers remained statistically significant across
(i) the stratified model (Appendix, Table 12), (ii) the full-sample model includ-
ing the interaction term (Table 3), and (iii) models adjusted for covariates
and the interaction term (Appendix, Table 13). Note that in (ii) and (iii),
we excluded the three-way interaction (Targeted × Information × Daily Meat
Consumer) for clarity and statistical robustness. Higher-order interactions
can be difficult to interpret without strong theoretical justification and add
unnecessary complexity. Additionally, estimating such interactions requires a
larger sample size to maintain statistical power, increasing the risk of over-
fitting. By focusing on main effects and two-way interactions, we provide a
clearer and more reliable analysis of how daily meat consumption influences
the impact of Targeted recommendations and Information. All models and
code are publicly available on the Open Science Framework project page (DOI:
https://osf.io/nb4vt/?view only=2d5ab97ba2ba4673843818f452098b3b).

Participants demonstrated a general willingness to engage with product
swap recommendations. On average, post-swap baskets exhibited a 24.9%
(SD = 15.7) reduction in GHGE compared to pre-swap baskets. Participants
swapped an average of 4.2 products (SD=2.8), and 88.4% of participants
swapped at least one product. In the post-shopping task survey (Appendix,
Table 7), 72.2% of participants agreed with the statement, ”I think it would be
good to receive such suggestions for alternative products with a lower carbon
footprint when shopping.”
3.1.1 Greenhouse gas emissions reduced
For the primary dependent variable, percentage GHGE reduction, the regres-
sion model (Table 2 and Figure 2) indicated a significant intercept of 23%
(p ¡ 0.001), suggesting that participants in the reference condition (Tar-
geted = No, Information = No) already exhibited a substantial reduction
in their basket GHGE. This baseline reduction indicates that, even in the
absence of the Targeted and Information treatments, participants engaged
in more climate-friendly purchasing behaviour after receiving product swap
recommendations.
The regression analysis did not reveal any statistically significant effects of
the Targeted or Information treatments on GHGE reduction compared to the
reference group (Targeted = No, Information = No).

3.2 Exploratory analyses
In addition to the preregistered analyses, we tested whether the Targeted and
Information treatments had any effects on the subgroup daily meat consumers.
In the reference group, consumers with daily meat consumption exhibited less
climate-friendly behaviours compared with participants with less than daily
meat consumption (Table 3 and Figure 3). Their post-swap basket GHGE were
11.5 percentage points higher, they had 65% lower odds of selecting the most
effective swap and swapped 50% fewer products. The percentage of their meat
and dairy consumption they were willing to swap for plant-based alternatives
was significantly lower (28 percentage points less for meat, 12 percentage points
less for dairy), and they reported significantly lower self-efficacy and response-
efficacy regarding their ability to reduce animal product consumption.
Despite these lower baseline measures, the Information treatment led to
significant improvements in both shopping task and post-task survey outcomes
amongst daily meat consumers (Table 3). Compared to daily meat consumers
that did not receive GHGE reduction information, those in the Information
condition reduced their basket GHGE by an additional 6.3 percentage points
(an increase of almost 50%), swapped 1.5 times more products, were more
willing to swap meat for plant-based alternatives (+11.6 percentage points,
an increase of over 50%), and reported higher self-efficacy in their ability to
partially reduce animal product consumption.

4 Discussion
The transition to more sustainable diets requires shifting consumption pat-
terns away from animal-based foods toward plant-based alternatives. Research
on consumer dietary guidance consistently shows that individuals prefer rec-
ommendations that are specific, actionable, and relevant to their daily lives
[26, 27]. In this study, we developed and tested a dietary intervention strat-
egy based on climate-friendly product swap recommendations designed to be
highly specific and actionable.
Additionally, simulation-based studies have demonstrated that small, tar-
geted dietary modifications can significantly reduce GHGE associated with
food consumption [2, 24, 28]. Building on these findings, we examine whether
targeted product swap recommendations — which target the most effective
GHGE-reducing product swap in a shopping basket — and the provision of
GHGE reduction information enhance consumer adoption of climate-friendly
food choices.
Our results indicate that offering specific and actionable product swap rec-
ommendations, derived from the final contents of baskets and presented before
checkout, is an effective strategy to support environmentally friendlier food
choices (H1). Almost 90% of participants swapped at least one product and
on average reduced the GHGE of their basket by approximately one-quarter.
Additionally, participants responded favourably to receiving such recommen-
dations, with almost three-quarters agreeing that they would find it good to
receive product swap recommendations while shopping.
In our randomized controlled trial, we investigated whether recommenda-
tions targeting the most effective GHGE-reducing product swap, by promi-
nently highlighting it as being the most effective at reducing their basket’s
GHGE, influenced consumer behaviour and lead to more climate friendly bas-
kets. Targeting the most effective product swap did increase the odds of it
being selected, but this did not translate into a significantly greater reduction
in overall basket GHGE (H2). The key advantage of targeted recommendations
is that consumers can achieve meaningful reductions with a single, strategic
change. However, participants in our study accepted an average of four swaps,
which may have diluted the impact of highlighting a single most-effective swap.
We also investigated whether providing GHGE reduction information for
swap amplifies the effect of specific and actionable product swap recommenda-
tions. However, similar to the targeted swap approach, the provision of GHGE
reduction information did not result in significantly lower basket GHGE for
most participants (H3). Furthermore, we found no evidence that the effective-
ness of targeted recommendations was enhanced by the inclusion of GHGE
reduction information (H4).
Several covariates emerged as significant predictors of basket GHGE. Male
gender and increasing age were associated with higher GHGE. Additionally,
higher meat and dairy consumption strongly predicted higher basket GHGE,
which aligns with the nature of our intervention—recommending swaps from
meat and dairy products to plant-based alternatives. It is therefore expected

20
that participants with higher baseline consumption of these products were less
likely to adopt the swaps, resulting in higher retained GHGE.
Daily meat consumption, in particular, was a strong predictor of less
climate-friendly shopping, as well as lower perceived self-efficacy and response-
efficacy regarding the reduction of animal product consumption. Given that
daily meat consumers are among those with the highest dietary carbon emis-
sions, they represent a crucial subgroup for dietary interventions. Recognising
their lower baseline engagement, we conducted post hoc exploratory analyses
to assess the effect of our interventions on this subgroup.
Our exploratory analyses revealed that GHGE reduction information had
a notably strong impact on daily meat consumers. Compared to those who
did not receive this information, daily meat consumers who received GHGE
reduction information shopped approximately 50% more climate-friendly.
Specifically, they reduced their basket GHGE by an additional 6.3 percentage
points (an increase of approximately 50%), swapped 1.5 times more products,
and expressed a willingness to replace 11.6 percentage points more meat prod-
ucts with plant-based alternatives (another increase of approximately 50%).
Additionally, they reported improved self-efficacy in reducing their animal
product consumption. As these findings on daily meat consumers were derived
from post hoc exploratory analyses rather than our preregistered hypotheses,
they should be interpreted with caution. Future studies should confirm these
results using preregistered designs to ensure robustness. To enhance the relia-
bility of our findings, we report only results where the effect of GHGE reduction
information on daily meat consumers remained statistically significant across
(i) the stratified model, (ii) the full-sample model including the interaction
term, and (iii) models adjusted for covariates and the interaction term.
These findings suggest that GHGE reduction information, when combined
with specific and actionable swap recommendations, may be a critical tool for
engaging high meat consumers, who require the largest dietary shifts to meet
sustainability targets. While specific and actionable product swap recommen-
dations on their own (i.e. without the need for GHGE reduction information
or targeted recommendations) may be sufficient for consumers already inclined
toward plant-based choices, information-based interventions appear to be par-
ticularly helpful to encourage behaviour change among those less receptive to
dietary modifications.
This study contributes to the broader literature on food choice interven-
tions by demonstrating that real-time, specific and actionable product swap
recommendations can effectively encourage climate-friendlier purchases. The
approach offers several advantages: recommendations are based on the con-
tents of a customer’s basket and delivered at the point of decision-making,
making them highly relevant; they are specific (e.g., swap Product A for Prod-
uct B) rather than general (e.g., reduce beef consumption); and they are highly
actionable, as accepting a swap is as simple as clicking a button.

21
From a policy and retail perspective, our findings suggest a practical and
scalable strategy for encouraging sustainable dietary choices. While imple-
mentations incorporating targeted recommendations and GHGE reduction
information depend on access to reliable environmental impact data—which
can be difficult to obtain and verify—our results indicate that simply offer-
ing specific and actionable product swaps from animal-based to plant-based
alternatives is sufficient to achieve meaningful GHGE reductions for most con-
sumers. This simplifies implementation for retailers, who only need to identify
appropriate product swaps and integrate them into the shopping experience.
The straightforward nature of this intervention, particularly when imple-
mented without targeted strategies or GHGE information, makes it highly
feasible for retailers operating online platforms or self-checkout systems.
A key consideration is whether the high effectiveness of basic product swap
recommendations observed in this study is partially driven by a novelty effect.
Participants swapped an average of four products — a substantial proportion
of the 11 available swaps — suggesting strong initial engagement. However, as
consumers become accustomed to swap recommendations, the novelty effect
may diminish, potentially leading to lower swap adoption over time. While
targeted recommendations did not lead to stronger effects in this study on
basket GHGE, they did increase the uptake of the most effective swap. In
such cases, if swap adoption decreases, swapping just one product more be a
more feasible and sustainable long-term behaviour change, while the targeted
recommendation ensures this one change is a meaningful one. Similarly, while
GHGE reduction information did not lead to stronger effects in this study on
basket GHGE, its long-term impact on consumer decision-making warrants
further exploration. GHGE reduction information may empower consumers
to make informed given their personal decision making factors (taste, price,
nutrition, etc.).
Importantly, our exploratory analyses suggest that GHGE reduction
information significantly influenced the effectiveness of product swap recom-
mendations among high meat consumers. As this group represents a key
demographic for achieving substantial dietary carbon footprint reductions, fur-
ther research is needed to evaluate the long-term efficacy of GHGE information
in shifting their purchasing behaviours.
This study has several strengths. First, we move beyond previous
simulation-based research on small, targeted dietary interventions by test-
ing our strategy in an experimental online supermarket setting. Second, we
take findings from consumer dietary guidance research, that consumers pre-
fer specific, actionable and personally-relevant dietary change advice, and
translate them into highly specific, highly actionable product swap recom-
mendations that can be delivered in real-time when purchasing decisions are
being made, and investigate their effect on consumer behaviours. Third, the
experiment was incentive-compatible and conducted in a realistic shopping
environment modelled on a major German retailer’s product portfolio. Fourth,
the robust experimental design allowed us to isolate the effects of targeted
recommendations and GHGE reduction information.

22
Despite these strengths, certain limitations must be acknowledged. First,
our sample was restricted to German-speaking, non-vegan/non-vegetarian
participants, and was over-represented by young male participants, limiting
generalisability. Second, our swap recommendations did not account for nutri-
tional aspects, which should be considered in future studies. Third, we only
examined swaps from animal-based to plant-based alternatives, whereas other
lower-carbon alternatives (e.g., swapping beef for chicken) may also be effective
[2]. Fourth, our study focused exclusively on GHGE, without incorporating
other environmental considerations such as water use or biodiversity impact.
Finally, while our experimental design sought to mimic real-world shopping
behaviour and was incentive-compatible, actual consumer decisions may differ
outside a controlled setting.
Our findings highlight product swap recommendations as a promising
tool for promoting sustainable food choices. Future research should exam-
ine their long-term impact in real-world retail settings and explore how they
interact with other behavioural interventions, such as financial incentives,
social norms, or policy regulations. Additionally, integrating nutritional con-
siderations alongside environmental impact assessments could enhance the
effectiveness and appeal of swap recommendations.
This study demonstrates that providing consumers with specific and action-
able product swap recommendations — based on their final basket contents
and presented before checkout — is an effective strategy for promoting climate-
friendly food choices. While this approach is sufficient for most consumers,
GHGE reduction information plays a crucial role in engaging high meat con-
sumers, a key demographic that needs addressing for achieving reducing the
carbon emissions of the food system.

Driving Sustainable Food Choices: The
Impact of Specific and Actionable Product
Swap Recommendations.

*Corresponding author(s). E-mail(s): kosullivan@ethz.ch;
Contributing authors: verena.tiefenbeck@fau.de;
sybilla.merian@business.uzh.ch; sabrina.stoeckli@business.uzh.ch;
efleisch@ethz.ch; martin.natter@business.uzh.ch;
Abstract
Dietary choices significantly impact both human health and the environ-
ment, with food-related greenhouse gas emissions (GHGE) constituting
a major contributor to climate change. While broad dietary guidelines
advocate for reducing animal-based food consumption, these recom-
mendations often lack the specific and actionable direction to motivate
behaviour change. This study examines the effectiveness of specific and
actionable product swap recommendations - proposing plant-based alter-
natives in place of animal-based products - within an experimental
1

2
online supermarket setting. We further assess whether (1) a recom-
mendation targeting the most effective GHGE-reducing swap and (2)
proving GHGE reduction information alongside these recommendations
enhances their impact. Participants were overall receptive to receiv-
ing product swap recommendations. Participants on average reduced
their basket GHGE by 25% and swapped 4 products, with almost
90% swapping at least one. The targeted recommendation increased
the uptake of the most effective swap, but neither targeted recommen-
dations nor GHGE reduction translated into significantly lower basket
GHGE for the majority of participants. Exploratory analyses suggest
that GHGE reduction information has a notably positive impact on
daily meat consumers, resulting in lower basket GHGE, more prod-
ucts swapped, an increased willingness-to-swap meat products and in
increase in their self-efficacy to reduce animal-product consumption.
These findings suggest that offering consumers the option to swap prod-
ucts—without the need for targeted recommendations or GHGE informa-
tion—may already be sufficient to encourage more sustainable purchasing
behaviours for many. However, to influence high-impact consumers,
particularly those with frequent meat consumption, providing GHGE
reduction information may be necessary to facilitate behaviour change.
1 Introduction

3
of specific and actionable direction to trigger behaviour change [26, 27] and
often demand drastic and unrealistic dietary changes [24].
An alternative approach is promoting small, targeted dietary changes. Such
modifications are often more feasible for consumers, cater to a broader audi-
ence, and enhance self-efficacy compared to more extreme dietary shifts, such
as adopting vegetarian or vegan diets [2]. Simulation-based studies suggest
that even minor dietary adjustments, such as replacing 10% of beef-derived
caloric intake with select plant-based foods [24] or substituting high-carbon
with lower-carbon meats (e.g., chicken instead of beef) [2], can achieve substan-
tial reductions in dietary carbon footprints (33–35%) while yielding meaningful
health co-benefits.
Consumers prefer dietary guidance that is specific, actionable, and relevant
to their daily lives [26, 27]. Research on the Dietary Guidelines for Ameri-
cans, for instance, found that abstract recommendations — such as limiting
fat intake to 30% of total calories — are perceived as impractical, as consumers
do not want to perform complex calculations when making food choices [26].
In this regard, small targeted changes need to be translatable into meaning-
ful specific and actionable guidance. For instance, while consumers can benefit
both environmentally and nutritionally by “substituting 10% of caloric intake
from beef and processed meat for fruits, vegetables, nuts, legumes and selected
seafood” [24], working in caloric percentages is impractical and not a guideline
that consumers could easily follow [26]. Consumers favour clear specific direc-
tions that are meaningful to their lives that do not require calculations [26],
such as product swap recommendations [2, 27].
Simulation-based studies suggest that targeted product swap recommen-
dations hold significant potential for reducing dietary GHGE [2, 28]. A study
simulating product swaps using Swiss household grocery purchase data found
that swapping just one targeted animal-based product per shopping trip could
reduce basket GHGE by nearly 30% on average (for baskets containing animal-
based products) and lower overall household GHGE from food purchases by
26% [28]. The targeted product swap recommendation is derived from the final
contents of a shopping basket and targets the product that, when swapped,
would result in the greatest GHGE reduction. Comparatively, the second and
third most effective swaps only reduced household GHGE by 7% and 3%,
respectively [28].
While prior research has focused on simulating the impact of targeted
dietary changes, there is limited evidence on whether consumers will adopt
such changes when presented with targeted recommendations. Field evidence
from the energy sector suggests that targeted, high-impact interventions —
such as strategies focused on water heating and air-conditioning — result
in greater reductions in energy consumption than interventions addressing a
broad set of activities, such as reducing total household electricity use [29, 30].
However, dietary behaviour presents unique challenges, and it remains unclear
whether targeted dietary recommendations will be more effective in driving
behaviour change compared to offering a broader set of substitution options.

2 Methods
2.1 Design and procedure
To investigate the role the pre-checkout product swap recommendations to
reduce consumer food GHGE, and in particular, the role of offering targeted
swap recommendations and the role of providing GHGE reduction informa-
tion, we conducted a 2 x 2, between-subject, randomised controlled trial in
a simulated online supermarket environment. The study was pregistered and
incentive compatible. The study was ran over a period of 11 weeks. The study
and four experimental conditions were designed to investigate the following
hypotheses:
H1 Participants shop more climate-friendly after receiving product swap
recommendations from animal-based products to plant-based products.
H2 Participants shop more climate-friendly when the most effective GHGE
reducing product swap is highlighted compared to just offering product swap
recommendations from animal-based products to plant-based products.
H3 Participants shop more climate-friendly when the GHGE reduction
information of each product swap is displayed compared to just offering
product swap recommendations from animal-based products to plant-based
products.
H4 Participants shop more climate-friendly when the most effective GHGE
reducing product swap is highlighted, and this effect is stronger when the
GHGE reduction information of each product swap is displayed.
An initial survey was used to determine eligibility for the study and to
gather demographic, dietary and grocery purchasing data, and to randomise
participants to one of the four experimental conditions. At the end of the ini-
tial survey, eligible participants were informed about the shopping task and the
online supermarket. For incentive compatibility, participants were informed
that 10 participants would be randomly selected to receive the products they
purchased in the online supermarket, and as such, should choose their prod-
ucts carefully. The initial survey finished with an attention check to ensure
that participants understood there was a chance that they could receive the
products they chose. Upon passing the attention check, participants were redi-
rected to the online shopping platform for the shopping task.
The shopping task consisted of participants being presented a pre-selected
basket of 21 products representing the average German basket of a 2-person
household over a one-week period [38], covering cereals, meat, fish, dairy, eggs,
fruit, and vegetables. All products and product data, such as price, were taken
directly from a major German brick-and-mortar retailer that also has an online
supermarket. The look and feel of the online supermarket was also modelled on
the same retailers. Participants were instructed to proceed through the online
supermarket to checkout, as if they were doing their weekly grocery shopping.
Prior to checkout, participants landed on the intervention page where there was
an explanation on how swapping animal-based products for plant-based prod-
ucts can meaningfully reduce the environmental impact of their food choices,

8
and in addition, participants were then presented with a list of recommended
swaps from the 11 animal-based products in their basket to plant-based alter-
native products according to their prescribed experimental condition (outlined
below). Participants could select as many of the available product swaps as
they desired.
After the swaps recommendations intervention, participants were brought
to a final checkout page where their final basket was presented and completed
the shopping. Upon completion, participants were automatically redirected
to a post-task survey which was used to collect information on the par-
ticipants’ shopping experience, environmental concerns, willingness-to-swap
(WTS) products, familiarity with the swap recommendation products, rea-
sons why they did and did not swap products, as well as self-efficacy and
response-efficacy concerning reducing animal-product consumption. Partici-
pants received 3 GBP as compensation for a median study duration time of
approximately 12 minutes.
Greenhouse gas emissions data for products were adapted from [28], where
they were estimated using a bottom-up life cycle assessment (LCA) that inte-
grated data from product-specific sources and life cycle inventory databases.
The impact assessment for GHG emissions was derived from the Global Warm-
ing Potential (GWP) 100a [4], which takes into account all GHG emissions
that contribute to climate change, and for a time horizon of 100 years, each
greenhouse gas (carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide) is compared with the
climate impact of carbon dioxide and expressed in carbon dioxide equivalents.
A detailed description of the LCA methodology can be found in [28].
Greenhouse gas emissions data for products were assigned using a bottom-
up life cycle assessment using information fro products and life cycle inventory
databases adapted from [28]. The impact assessment for GHG emissions was
derived from the Global Warming Potential (GWP) 100a [4], which takes into
account all GHG emissions that contribute to climate change, and for a time
horizon of 100 years, each greenhouse gas (carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous
oxide) is compared with the climate impact of carbon dioxide and expressed in
carbon dioxide equivalents. Detailed explanation on the life cycle assessment
are provided in [28].
The study was approved by the University of Zurich Ethics Commis-
sion. The preregistration and the data of this study are publicly available
on the Open Science Framework project page (DOI: https://osf.io/nb4vt/
?view only=2d5ab97ba2ba4673843818f452098b3b). The study was conducted
online between July 28th and October 15th, 2023.
2.2 Participants
A sample of German-speaking participants was recruited via online panels
managed by Prolific. Preregistered exclusion criteria included (i) a minimum
age of 16 years, (ii) identify with a diet that restrict the consumption of animal
products (i.e. vegan or vegetarian), (iii) an answer of “never” for items con-
cerning their consumption frequency of dairy products and meat products, (iv)

9
failed attention checks, and (v) did not complete the pre-task survey, shopping
task, or post-task survey. Additionally, after data collection, we excluded non-
binary participants (N = 12) due to their low representation in the sample,
which prevented reliable statistical estimation.
The required sample size was calculated with a power of 0.8 and α of 0.05
to detect a small effect size (f2 = 0.02) with 3 predictors. This gives a total
sample size of 863 participants. To account for dropouts and missing data, we
increased the sample size to 1200 participants. Of these 1200 participants, 2 did
not complete the initial survey and 96 were excluded due to not meeting the
inclusion criteria. 1059 of these eligible participants completed the shopping
task and all of these participants completed the post-task survey. Table 4 shows
the demographic characteristics of the sample.
2.3 Intervention and experimental conditions
Participants were randomly exposed to one of four experimental conditions
of a 2 x 2 experimental design on the product swap recommendation page:
Targeted(Yes vs No) and Information(Yes vs. No), shown in Figure 1. In our
preregistration, we referred to the Targeted treatment as “Generic” vs. “Tar-
geted” and the Information treatment as “Without Information” vs. “With
Information”. In this manuscript, we use the new terminology “Targeted (No
vs. Yes)” and “Information (No vs. Yes)” for clarity and to better reflect the
nature of the interventions and their implementation in the statistical models.
The underlying conditions and experimental design remain unchanged.
Participants in all experimental conditions were exposed to the swap rec-
ommendation intervention that (1) explained how swapping animal-based
products for plant-based products can meaningfully reduce the environmental
impact of their food choices, and (2) presented a list of recommended swaps
from the 11 animal-based products in their basket to plant-based alterna-
tive products. The Targeted(Yes vs. No) treatments differed in that the most
effective GHGE reducing product swap (i.e., the targeted swap) was explic-
itly highlighted as being the most effective at reducing basket GHGE in the
Targeted(Yes) treatment. The Information(Yes vs. No) treatments differed in
that the percentage GHGE reduction that would occur from the swap was
displayed alongside each swap in the Information(Yes) treatment. The swap
recommendations were from the original animal-based product to it’s closest
second generation plant-based analogue. For example, plant-based sausages
were the recommended swap from pork-based sausages, and soy-based yoghurt
was the recommended swap from milk-based yoghurt. The recommended swap
products were chosen to be as close as possible in terms of product weight to
the original product in the basket (e.g. 500g of milk-based yoghurt could be
swapped for 500g of soy-based sausages). Where this was not possible, multi-
ple packages of the recommended swap product were recommended to match
the weight of the original product in the basket (e.g. a 350g package of chicken
could be swapped for two 180g packages of plant-based chicken).

10
2.4 Measures
The primary dependent variable was basket GHGE reduction following the
product swap recommendations intervention. This was calculated by determin-
ing the difference in GHGE of the initial basket (i.e. before the product swap
recommendations page intervention) and the final basket (i.e. after product
swap recommendations page intervention). The secondary dependent variables
were a binary variable for whether participants chose the targeted product
swap recommendation (i.e. the product recommendation that is highlighted in
Targeted treatment) and reported self-efficacy and response-efficacy regarding
reducing their animal product consumption. The items on perceived self-
efficacy and response-efficacy items were adapted from [39] and participants
were asked to indicate the level of agreement on a 7 point Likert scale from 1
(“totally disagree”) to 7 (“totally agree”). Item text are provided in the tables
reporting the results in the Appendix (Table 8 and Table 10).
Other preregistered exploratory variables included: receptivity to receiving
recommendations for alternative products with a lower their carbon footprint
when shopping (1 = “not at all” to 7 = “completely”); how well the supermar-
ket informed participants about which food in your shopping basket can reduce
their carbon footprint the most or the least (1 = “informed very poorly” to 7 =
“informed very well”); how well the supermarket informed participants about
the percentage reduction in carbon footprint that could achieved through each
product swap recommendation (1 = “informed very poorly” to 7 = “informed
very well”); percentage of their meat consumption they would be would be
willing to swap for plant-based alternatives (slider scale from 0 to 100); per-
centage of their dairy consumption they would be would be willing to swap
for plant-based alternatives (slider scale from 0 to 100).
In addition to the preregistered exploratory variables, we also report the
number of products that participants swapped and the number of participants
that swapped at least one product.

4 Discussion
The transition to more sustainable diets requires shifting consumption pat-
terns away from animal-based foods toward plant-based alternatives. Research
on consumer dietary guidance consistently shows that individuals prefer rec-
ommendations that are specific, actionable, and relevant to their daily lives
[26, 27]. In this study, we developed and tested a dietary intervention strat-
egy based on climate-friendly product swap recommendations designed to be
highly specific and actionable.
Additionally, simulation-based studies have demonstrated that small, tar-
geted dietary modifications can significantly reduce GHGE associated with
food consumption [2, 24, 28]. Building on these findings, we examine whether
targeted product swap recommendations — which target the most effective
GHGE-reducing product swap in a shopping basket — and the provision of
GHGE reduction information enhance consumer adoption of climate-friendly
food choices.
Our results indicate that offering specific and actionable product swap rec-
ommendations, derived from the final contents of baskets and presented before
checkout, is an effective strategy to support environmentally friendlier food
choices (H1). Almost 90% of participants swapped at least one product and
on average reduced the GHGE of their basket by approximately one-quarter.
Additionally, participants responded favourably to receiving such recommen-
dations, with almost three-quarters agreeing that they would find it good to
receive product swap recommendations while shopping.
In our randomized controlled trial, we investigated whether recommenda-
tions targeting the most effective GHGE-reducing product swap, by promi-
nently highlighting it as being the most effective at reducing their basket’s
GHGE, influenced consumer behaviour and lead to more climate friendly bas-
kets. Targeting the most effective product swap did increase the odds of it
being selected, but this did not translate into a significantly greater reduction
in overall basket GHGE (H2). The key advantage of targeted recommendations
is that consumers can achieve meaningful reductions with a single, strategic
change. However, participants in our study accepted an average of four swaps,
which may have diluted the impact of highlighting a single most-effective swap.
We also investigated whether providing GHGE reduction information for
swap amplifies the effect of specific and actionable product swap recommenda-
tions. However, similar to the targeted swap approach, the provision of GHGE
reduction information did not result in significantly lower basket GHGE for
most participants (H3). Furthermore, we found no evidence that the effective-
ness of targeted recommendations was enhanced by the inclusion of GHGE
reduction information (H4).
Several covariates emerged as significant predictors of basket GHGE. Male
gender and increasing age were associated with higher GHGE. Additionally,
higher meat and dairy consumption strongly predicted higher basket GHGE,
which aligns with the nature of our intervention—recommending swaps from
meat and dairy products to plant-based alternatives. It is therefore expected

21
From a policy and retail perspective, our findings suggest a practical and
scalable strategy for encouraging sustainable dietary choices. While imple-
mentations incorporating targeted recommendations and GHGE reduction
information depend on access to reliable environmental impact data—which
can be difficult to obtain and verify—our results indicate that simply offer-
ing specific and actionable product swaps from animal-based to plant-based
alternatives is sufficient to achieve meaningful GHGE reductions for most con-
sumers. This simplifies implementation for retailers, who only need to identify
appropriate product swaps and integrate them into the shopping experience.
The straightforward nature of this intervention, particularly when imple-
mented without targeted strategies or GHGE information, makes it highly
feasible for retailers operating online platforms or self-checkout systems.
A key consideration is whether the high effectiveness of basic product swap
recommendations observed in this study is partially driven by a novelty effect.
Participants swapped an average of four products — a substantial proportion
of the 11 available swaps — suggesting strong initial engagement. However, as
consumers become accustomed to swap recommendations, the novelty effect
may diminish, potentially leading to lower swap adoption over time. While
targeted recommendations did not lead to stronger effects in this study on
basket GHGE, they did increase the uptake of the most effective swap. In
such cases, if swap adoption decreases, swapping just one product more be a
more feasible and sustainable long-term behaviour change, while the targeted
recommendation ensures this one change is a meaningful one. Similarly, while
GHGE reduction information did not lead to stronger effects in this study on
basket GHGE, its long-term impact on consumer decision-making warrants
further exploration. GHGE reduction information may empower consumers
to make informed given their personal decision making factors (taste, price,
nutrition, etc.).
Importantly, our exploratory analyses suggest that GHGE reduction
information significantly influenced the effectiveness of product swap recom-
mendations among high meat consumers. As this group represents a key
demographic for achieving substantial dietary carbon footprint reductions, fur-
ther research is needed to evaluate the long-term efficacy of GHGE information
in shifting their purchasing behaviours.
This study has several strengths. First, we move beyond previous
simulation-based research on small, targeted dietary interventions by test-
ing our strategy in an experimental online supermarket setting. Second, we
take findings from consumer dietary guidance research, that consumers pre-
fer specific, actionable and personally-relevant dietary change advice, and
translate them into highly specific, highly actionable product swap recom-
mendations that can be delivered in real-time when purchasing decisions are
being made, and investigate their effect on consumer behaviours. Third, the
experiment was incentive-compatible and conducted in a realistic shopping
environment modelled on a major German retailer’s product portfolio. Fourth,
the robust experimental design allowed us to isolate the effects of targeted
recommendations and GHGE reduction information.
